title: Lecture 4 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 04.


See the formula
\[P_X(x) = P(\{\omega : X(\omega) \le x\})\]
on a tiny example (coin), then estimate a CDF from samples.
Run with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print('Ready')




Fair coin:

Omega = {H, T}
P({H}) = P({T}) = 1/2
Random variable X: X(H)=1, X(T)=0


Omega = {"H", "T"}

def P(event):
    event = set(event)
    return sum(0.5 for o in event if o in Omega)

def X(omega):
    return 1.0 if omega == "H" else 0.0

print("P({H}) =", P({"H"}))
print("X(H), X(T) =", X("H"), X("T"))




For a number x, look at the event {omega : X(omega) <= x}, then apply P.
That is exactly P_X(x) from the lecture.

def P_X(x):
    """CDF / distribution function of X at real number x."""
    event = {omega for omega in Omega if X(omega) <= x}
    return P(event)

for x in [-1, 0, 0.5, 1, 2]:
    print(f"P_X({x}) = P(X <= {x}) = {P_X(x)}")




For x < 0: nothing maps to <= x → probability 0

For 0 <= x < 1: only T (value 0) → probability 1/2

For x >= 1: both outcomes → probability 1

That step function is the pushforward / distribution of X.




In ML we rarely know P. We observe many values of X (range samples) and estimate.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
# simulate abstract outcomes, push through X (like a sensor)
samples = np.array([X(o) for o in rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=n)])

xs = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 200)
# empirical CDF: fraction of samples <= x
ecdf = np.array([(samples <= x).mean() for x in xs])
true = np.array([P_X(x) for x in xs])

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.step(xs, true, where="post", label="true P_X (from Omega)")
plt.plot(xs, ecdf, label="empirical CDF from samples")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("P(X <= x)")
plt.title("Pushforward distribution of coin RV X")
plt.legend()
plt.show()





# Exercise A: unfair coin P(H)=0.7, same X coding.
# Recompute P_X at x = -1, 0, 0.5, 1.

def P_unfair(event, p_h=0.7):
    event = set(event)
    mass = {"H": p_h, "T": 1 - p_h}
    return sum(mass[o] for o in event)

def P_X_unfair(x):
    event = {o for o in Omega if X(o) <= x}
    return P_unfair(event)

for x in [-1, 0, 0.5, 1]:
    print(x, P_X_unfair(x))


# Exercise B: die, X(omega)=omega.
# What is P_X(3.5)? (should equal P(X <= 3.5) = P({1,2,3}) = 3/6)

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

def P_die(event):
    return len(set(event) & Omega_die) / len(Omega_die)

def P_X_die(x):
    event = {o for o in Omega_die if o <= x}
    return P_die(event)

print("P_X(3.5) =", P_X_die(3.5))

In this notebook

{omega : X(omega) <= x}


Pushforward / P_X
P of that event


Work with samples
empirical CDF approximates P_X

title: Lecture 2 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 02.


Feel these ideas with tiny examples:

Random experiment → you choose what it is
Sample space Ω → all outcomes
Events → subsets of Ω
Probability measure P → numbers in [0,1] with simple rules

Run cells top to bottom with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np

print("Ready")




Lecture point: the experiment is your design choice.
We take: one fair coin toss.
Outcomes are not numbers yet — just labels.

Omega = {"H", "T"}  # sample space
print("Sample space Ω =", Omega)
print("Number of outcomes =", len(Omega))







Event (English)
As a set




Heads
{H}


Tails
{T}


Anything
{H, T} = Ω


Impossible
empty set = ∅




event_heads = {"H"}
event_tails = {"T"}
event_anything = Omega
event_impossible = set()

print("Heads event:", event_heads)
print("Impossible event:", event_impossible)




For a fair coin:

P({H}) = P({T}) = 1/2
P(Ω) = 1
P(∅) = 0

Check lecture properties: non-negative, P(Ω)=1, disjoint additivity.

def P_fair_coin(event):
    """Probability of an event for a fair coin (event subset of {H,T})."""
    event = set(event)
    if not event.issubset(Omega):
        raise ValueError("Event must be a subset of Omega")
    # fair: each singleton outcome has mass 1/2
    return sum(0.5 for outcome in event)

print("P(H) =", P_fair_coin({"H"}))
print("P(T) =", P_fair_coin({"T"}))
print("P(Omega) =", P_fair_coin(Omega))
print("P(empty) =", P_fair_coin(set()))

# Disjoint additivity: H and T do not overlap
print("P(H)+P(T) =", P_fair_coin({"H"}) + P_fair_coin({"T"}))




Same physical coin, new experiment: toss twice.
Ω₂ = {HH, HT, TH, TT}
This matches the lecture: you choose the experiment.

Omega2 = {"HH", "HT", "TH", "TT"}
print("Two-toss sample space:", Omega2)

# Event: exactly one head
exactly_one_head = {o for o in Omega2 if o.count("H") == 1}
print("Exactly one head:", exactly_one_head)

# Fair independent tosses -> each of 4 outcomes has probability 1/4
P_exact = len(exactly_one_head) / len(Omega2)
print("P(exactly one head) =", P_exact)




Lecture: when physics is hard, repeat observations and use statistics.
Simulate many fair tosses; the fraction of heads should approach 1/2.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 10_000
tosses = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=n)
frac_heads = np.mean(tosses == "H")

print(f"In {n} tosses, fraction of heads ≈ {frac_heads:.3f}")
print("True P(H) for fair coin = 0.5")





# Exercise A: unfair coin with P(H)=0.7

def P_unfair(event, p_heads=0.7):
    event = set(event)
    mass = {"H": p_heads, "T": 1 - p_heads}
    return sum(mass[o] for o in event)

print("Unfair P(H) =", P_unfair({"H"}))
print("Unfair P(T) =", P_unfair({"T"}))
print("Unfair P(Omega) =", P_unfair({"H", "T"}))


# Exercise B: die Omega = {1,...,6}, fair — what is P(even)?

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
even = {2, 4, 6}
P_even = len(even) / len(Omega_die)
print("P(even) =", P_even)

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 2 — Multi-tenant thinking (roles)
GateKeeper-style platforms usually separate who administers the platform from who administers one tenant’s APIs.
Platform admin  → manage the platform itself
Tenant admin    → manage routes/policies for one tenant
API caller      → call routes with a JWT under that tenant’s rules
Plain words:

Not every authenticated user is an admin

Route policies can require roles (ROLE_ADMIN, tenant roles, …)

Management APIs are themselves protected (JWT + roles)

Exact role names follow the lecture’s code—learn the idea: platform vs tenant vs caller.

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 4 — Live request pipeline (Gateway)
Think in ordered stages (filters / interceptors / services—same story):
1. Correlation ID     (create or propagate X-Correlation-Id)
2. Route match        (memory registry)
3. JWT validate       (local signature + claims)
4. Role check         (route policy)
5. Rate limit         (Redis atomic)
6. Idempotency        (Redis; mainly configured POSTs)
7. Transform          (path rewrite, header add/remove)
8. Proxy forward      (HTTP to target + timeout)
9. Access event       (publish to Kafka)
10. Return response / gateway error
If a stage fails → consistent gateway error (do not leak stack traces to clients).

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 5 — API Management responsibilities (hands-on view)
Management is not on the hot path for every forward, but it is critical for:

Register / login → issue JWTs

CRUD for routes and policies

Versioning config

Auditing admin actions (AOP is a good fit: “when admin changes route, write audit row”)

Publishing configuration events

MySQL tables (conceptual): users, roles, routes, policy settings, versions, audits.
Other services must not UPDATE Management tables directly.

Dedup: consumers can see duplicates after retries → use unique eventId.
correlationId ties work for one client request; it is not the dedup key.

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1

Topic 1 — Why an API gateway?
Without a gateway, every client must know:

how to validate tokens everywhere

how to apply shared limits and correlation IDs

Gateway jobs:



Job
Meaning

AuthN/AuthZ, rate limits, idempotency, …


Reverse proxying
Forward HTTP and return the response



Forward proxy  → helps clients reach the internet
Reverse proxy  → sits in front of your servers
API gateway    → reverse proxy + API policies
Boundary rule: gateway handles entry rules. Target services still enforce business rules (who may change this order).

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
section: Topic 3 — Data plane vs control plane
text:
Topic 3 — Data plane vs control plane
Control plane (API Management)
  define routes, roles, limits
  store durable config in MySQL
  publish "config changed" events

Data plane (Smart Gateway)
  keep active routes in MEMORY
  validate JWT locally
  talk to Redis for shared counters
  forward to targets
  publish access events (async)
If Management is temporarily down, already loaded routes can still serve traffic. New admin changes wait until Management returns.

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
text:
Topic 4 — Latency design
A gateway always adds a hop. GateKeeper avoids extra synchronous calls:








Work
Where
Why




Route match
Gateway memory
No DB hit per request


JWT validate
Gateway process
No auth-service round trip each time


Rate limit / idempotency
Redis
Shared, fast state


Analytics store
Kafka → Analytics
Off the live response path



BAD:  every request → Management + Auth + Analytics + DB + target
GOOD: memory + local JWT + Redis if needed + target
      (+ Kafka fire-and-forget style analytics)

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Big idea in one line
“Login with Google” does not mean users type their Google password into your app.
Google authenticates them; your app receives permission (and identity) through a standard protocol: OAuth 2.0 (+ OpenID Connect for “who is this user?”).
User → Your app → redirect → Google login + consent
                         ← redirect back with code
Your app ↔ Google        exchange code → tokens
Your app                 create local session / your JWT

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
section: Topic 1 — Why not collect Google passwords?
text:
Topic 1 — Why not collect Google passwords?
If users gave you their Google password, you could open Drive, Photos, Mail, …
Nobody should do that. OAuth exists so Google stays the identity provider; you only get scoped access the user approved.

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 2 — Main actors







Actor
Plain role




Resource owner
The user


Client
Your application


Authorization server
Google (login + consent + codes/tokens)

Google APIs (Calendar, …) when you call them with an access token

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 3 — Scope and consent
Scope = what you ask for (openid, email, profile, or API scopes like calendar read).
Consent = Google shows the user a screen: “Allow this app to …?”
Ask fewer scopes → easier consent → less risk
Ask powerful scopes → user may refuse

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 4 — OAuth vs OpenID Connect (OIDC)









OAuth 2.0
OpenID Connect




Main job
Authorization — allow access to resources
Authentication — prove who logged in


Typical token
Access token
ID token (+ often access token too)


Question answered
“What may this client do?”
“Who is the user?”



For “Sign in with Google,” you want OIDC (login), not only “call Google Calendar.”
ID token     → for your app (identity claims: sub, email, …)
Access token → for calling Google APIs (if scopes allow)

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 5 — Authorization Code flow (browser apps)
Common happy path:

User clicks “Continue with Google”

Browser redirects to Google with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, …

User logs in + consents

Google redirects to your redirect_uri with an authorization code (+ state)

Your backend exchanges the code for tokens (server-side, with client secret when using confidential clients)

You create your own logged-in state (session or your JWT)

state parameter: random value you send and verify on return → helps stop CSRF on the redirect.

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
section: Topic 6 — PKCE (why mobile / public clients need it)
text:
Topic 6 — PKCE (why mobile / public clients need it)
PKCE (“pixy”) protects the authorization code when a client cannot keep a secret safe (SPA / mobile).
Before redirect:
  create code_verifier (random)
  create code_challenge = hash(verifier)
  send challenge to Google

Token exchange:
  send code + code_verifier
  Google checks verifier matches earlier challenge
Even if an attacker steals the redirect code, they lack the verifier → exchange fails.

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Big idea in one line
HTTP requests do not remember each other.
Stateful apps remember you with a server session. Stateless JWT apps remember you by sending a signed token on every request—and the server rebuilds Authentication from that token.
STATEFUL                         STATELESS (JWT)
────────                         ───────────────
login → create session           login → create JWT
cookie: session id               client stores token
next request: cookie             next request: Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
server loads session context     server verifies signature → builds Authentication

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 1 — Why sessions feel “sticky”
After form/basic login with sessions:

Server stores security info (or a pointer to it)
Browser sends session cookie automatically
Scale-out needs sticky sessions or shared session store

That works. APIs and mobile clients often prefer tokens instead.

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 2 — What a JWT is
JWT = JSON Web Token (often said “jot”).
Three parts separated by dots:
header.payload.signature







Part
Holds




Header
Algorithm + type (e.g. HS256, JWT)


Payload
Claims (sub, roles, exp, …) — readable (Base64), not secret


Signature
Proves the payload was not tampered with (needs server secret/key)



Anyone can decode payload
Only someone with the key can forge a valid signature
Important: default signed JWT is not encryption. Do not put passwords or secrets inside claims.
Related ideas (names only):

JWS — signed token (common API JWT)
JWE — encrypted token (different goal)

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 4 — Custom JWT filter (idea)
Place a filter before username/password filters:
Request
  → JwtAuthFilter
       if Bearer token present:
         parse + verify
         build Authentication
         SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...)
  → rest of chain
  → controller
If no token and URL is public → continue.
If token invalid → 401.
If valid → authorization rules use the authorities from the token/DB policy you chose.

Step 3 — Login endpoint
@PostMapping("/login")
public Map<String, String> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
    authenticationManager.authenticate(
        new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(req.username(), req.password())
    );
    String token = jwtService.generateToken(req.username());
    return Map.of("token", token);
}
Only issue a token after authentication succeeds.


Step 4 — Security config

Stateless sessions
CSRF disabled for token API demos
Permit /register, /login
Add JWT filter into the chain
anyRequest().authenticated()



Step 5 — Postman flow

Register user

Login → copy token

Call /api/secure with header Authorization: Bearer <token>

Tamper one character of the token → should fail signature check

Wait until exp passes → should fail as expired

Topic
Note




Logout
Server cannot “delete” a pure JWT easily; use short expiry + refresh strategy / blocklist if needed

Attacker can forge tokens until you rotate keys


Fat tokens
Huge payloads waste bandwidth; keep claims small


Revocation
Not free in pure stateless design

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Big idea in one line
You should not reinvent login as a random controller method.
Spring Security already has a pipeline: filter → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService → PasswordEncoder → SecurityContext.
POST credentials
      │
      ▼
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or your equivalent)
      │  builds Authentication (not yet trusted)
      ▼
AuthenticationManager
      │
      ▼
DaoAuthenticationProvider
      │  loadUserByUsername + password matches
      ▼
Authenticated Authentication
      │
      ▼
SecurityContextHolder  (saved for this request / session)

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 1 — Stop hand-rolled “fake login”
In earlier practice you may have written something like “check username/password in /login yourself.”
Problems:

Easy to forget hashing rules
Easy to forget setting SecurityContext
Easy to disagree with the rest of the filter chain (CSRF, session, logout, …)

Better: let Security’s authentication architecture own the verify step; your code supplies UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder + URL rules.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 2 — AuthenticationManager and providers
AuthenticationManager
   └── delegates to one or more AuthenticationProvider
            └── DaoAuthenticationProvider  (username/password + UserDetailsService)
DaoAuthenticationProvider (the one you use for DB login):

Call UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername
Use PasswordEncoder.matches
Check account flags (enabled, locked, …)
Return a fully authenticated Authentication with authorities

You rarely call the provider yourself. The manager does.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 3 — UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
Two common states of the same class:







State
Meaning




Unauthenticated token
principal = username, credentials = password


Authenticated token
principal = UserDetails, credentials cleared/null, authorities set



That is how a “claim” becomes a “verified identity.”

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 4 — Filter chain groups (mental model)
You do not memorize every filter name on day one. Group them:
1) Exploit protection   → CSRF, headers, …
2) Authentication       → prove identity / read credentials
3) Authorization        → allow or deny based on authorities
4) Misc / special       → logout, anonymous, exception translation, …
Request walks the chain. Fail early when needed. Success → controller.
CSRF note: browser form/session apps care a lot; pure Bearer-token APIs often disable CSRF when sessions are not used (JWT lecture next). Know why before copying a snippet.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 5 — What “login success” stores
After success:

Authenticated Authentication is created

Placed into SecurityContext

For stateful apps, the context is tied to an HTTP session (cookie) so the next request remembers you

Stateful:
  login once → session id cookie → later requests reuse SecurityContext

Next lecture (JWT):
  login once → token to client → each request sends token → rebuild Authentication

Step 2 — Security filter chain
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // OK for simple API demos; revisit for browsers+sessions
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/register", "/login").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated()
        )
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
        // or .formLogin(...) for browser form login
    return http.build();
}


Step 3 — Optional: expose AuthenticationManager
Useful when you later issue tokens after verifying credentials:
@Bean
AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration config) throws Exception {
    return config.getAuthenticationManager();
}

In a controller, print SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getAuthorities()

Expect

Wrong password

Example role rule:
.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring Security does not talk to your User entity directly.
You load users from the DB, wrap them as UserDetails, and store only hashed passwords (usually BCrypt).
Your table: users (id, username, password_hash, roles, …)
                │
                ▼
        UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(...)
                │
                ▼
           UserDetails   ← what Security understands
                │
                ▼
     PasswordEncoder matches raw password vs hash

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
section: Topic 1 — Why not store plain passwords?
text:
Topic 1 — Why not store plain passwords?
If the DB leaks and passwords are plain text → every account is stolen.
Even “fast hashes” are weak against modern cracking (GPUs + rainbow tables of common passwords).
Need:

One-way hash (cannot reverse to the original password)
Slow enough on purpose (limits guessing speed)
Salt (same password → different hash for different users)

BCrypt does slow hashing + salting for you.

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Topic 2 — PasswordEncoder
Spring Security’s interface:
@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
}



Method
When you use it




encode(raw)
Register / change password → store the result


matches(raw, encoded)
Login → compare typed password to DB hash



Never write your own “encrypt password with Base64.” That is encoding, not security.
Register:
  "secret123" ──encode──► "$2a$10$...."  ──save──► DB

Login:
  typed "secret123" + DB hash ──matches?──► true / false

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Topic 3 — UserDetails (Security’s user shape)
Security expects a UserDetails with roughly:

username
password (the hash)
authorities / roles
flags: account enabled? locked? expired? credentials expired?

Your JPA entity can stay as User.
You build a bridge (wrapper / adapter) that implements UserDetails and reads from that entity.
Entity User  ──wrap──►  CustomUserDetails implements UserDetails
Plain words: map your world to Security’s world.

Mistake
Fix




Save plain password
Always encode on register


Double-encode on login
Login uses matches, not encode again for storage

Be consistent: hasRole("USER") expects ROLE_USER


Forgetting unique username

Login    → load UserDetails → matches(raw, hash)

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Big idea in one line
Never trust the client.
Spring Security sits in front of your controllers, checks who you are (authentication) and what you may do (authorization), and stores that answer in a SecurityContext.
Client (browser / Postman / mobile)
        │
        ▼
   Tomcat / servlet container
        │
        ▼
   Spring Security filter chain   ← decide: allow / deny / challenge
        │
        ▼
   DispatcherServlet → Controllers

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
section: Why security is a server job
text:
Why security is a server job
A trust boundary is crossed when a request leaves one world and enters another (internet → your app).
Front-end tricks are not security:

Hide an “Admin” button in HTML → a user can still call /api/admin with Postman or curl
Client-side checks are UX, not protection

Rule: every protected action must be enforced on the server.

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Topic 1 — Authentication vs authorization








Word
Plain meaning
Guard analogy




Authentication
“Prove who you claim to be”
Show your employee ID at the gate


Authorization
“Are you allowed to do this?”
ID accepted, but you still cannot sit in the CEO office



Claim: "I am Aditya"
   │

   ▼

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 2 — Propagation cheat sheet



Mode
If TX already exists
If none




REQUIRED
Join it
Create one


REQUIRES_NEW
Suspend it; start new
Create one


SUPPORTS
Join it
Run with no TX


MANDATORY
Join it
Throw


NOT_SUPPORTED
Suspend; run without TX
Run without TX


NEVER
Throw
Run without TX


NESTED
Savepoint inside current
Create one



REQUIRED (default) — “be part of the caller’s unit of work”
REQUIRES_NEW       — “commit/rollback myself even if outer fails later”
NESTED             — “partial rollback via savepoint” (DB support matters)

Mental pictures
Outer REQUIRED
  └─ Inner REQUIRED     → same TX

Outer REQUIRED
  └─ Inner REQUIRES_NEW → inner commits alone; outer can still roll back its own work
Use REQUIRES_NEW for things like audit logs that must persist even when the business TX fails — carefully.

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 3 — Commit / rollback attributes







Attribute
Use




rollbackFor
Also roll back for these exception types (e.g. checked)


noRollbackFor
Do not roll back for these


readOnly
Hint: reads only (optimizations / intent)


timeout
Fail if TX runs too long (seconds)



@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void importFile() throws Exception {
    // checked exceptions also roll back
}

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 4 — Isolation levels (why they exist)
Concurrent transactions can cause:



Phenomenon
Plain meaning




Dirty read
See another TX’s uncommitted change


Non-repeatable read
Re-read a row; committed data changed


Phantom read
Re-query a range; new matching rows appear



Isolation ↑  →  fewer surprises, often more locking / less concurrency
Isolation ↓  →  more concurrency, more anomaly risk

Common levels







Level
Rough protection




READ_UNCOMMITTED
Allows dirty reads


READ_COMMITTED
No dirty reads (common default)


REPEATABLE_READ
Same row reads stay stable (phantoms depend on DB)


SERIALIZABLE
Strongest; transactions feel almost one-at-a-time



@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public void reportBalances() { }
Exact behaviour is database-specific. Always verify with your DB docs when tuning.

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 5 — Choosing attributes (practical)
Ask:

Should this method share the caller’s success/failure? → REQUIRED

Must this succeed independently? → REQUIRES_NEW

Is this read-mostly reporting? → readOnly = true (+ isolation if needed)

Do checked exceptions mean business failure? → rollbackFor

Do not crank isolation to SERIALIZABLE everywhere “to be safe.” Measure need vs throughput.

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Big idea in one line
Three separate knobs:

Cascade — if I persist/delete parent, should children follow?

Fetch type — load related data now or later?

Fetch plan per query — for this use case, what graph do I need? (EntityGraph / join fetch)

Cascade  ≠  ownership (mappedBy / JoinColumn)
Lazy     ≠  "never load"
EAGER    ≠  guaranteed single JOIN SQL

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 1 — Cascading
Cascade = propagate a persistence operation along a relationship.
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
private List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
order.addItem(item1);
order.addItem(item2);
em.persist(order); // also persists item1, item2 if PERSIST cascade

Cascade types



Type
Propagates




PERSIST
persist


MERGE
merge


REMOVE
remove


REFRESH
refresh


DETACH
detach


ALL
all of the above



Not on by default. Add only when lifecycles truly belong together (order + order lines). Avoid REMOVE on shared many-to-many (deleting a student must not delete a shared course).
Helper still required for owning side:
public void addItem(OrderItem item) {
    items.add(item);
    item.setOrder(this);
}

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 2 — Lazy vs Eager



Fetch
Meaning




LAZY
Load association when first needed (hint)


EAGER
Association must be available when entity is loaded




JPA defaults



Relationship
Default




@ManyToOne / @OneToOne
EAGER


@OneToMany / @ManyToMany
LAZY



Practical habit: make to-one LAZY too, then fetch explicitly per use case.
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "department_id")
private Department department;
find(Student)
  SELECT student columns...
  department = proxy (not loaded)

student.getDepartment().getName()
  SELECT department...   ← triggered now

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 3 — N+1 problem
Pattern:

1 query loads N parents

Loop touches a lazy association → up to N more queries

List<Student> students = // findAll students
for (Student s : students) {
    System.out.println(s.getDepartment().getName()); // may query each time
}
SELECT * FROM student;                 -- 1
SELECT * FROM department WHERE id=?;   -- +1 per distinct miss
...
L1 cache can reduce duplicates (100 students, 3 departments → maybe 1+3), but the design smell remains: relationship access hides SQL.
Same idea for collections:
SELECT * FROM department;                      -- 1
SELECT * FROM student WHERE department_id=1;   -- N times
Lazy is not the enemy. Missing a fetch plan for a known use case is.
Switching mapping to EAGER is a blunt fix: loads association even when unused, and may still use extra selects.

spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
Run the loop. Count statements. If you see repeats inside a for-loop, you found N+1.

EntityManager is not “just a SQL helper.”

@Service method (@Transactional)
        │
        ▼
 persistence context (1st-level cache)
   map of managed entities
        │
        ▼
 flush → SQL to DB
        │
        ▼
 commit → DB transaction ends

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 2 — Persistence context
Plain meaning: Hibernate’s memory of entities it is currently managing.







Question
Answer




Where do managed entities live?
Persistence context


How long?
Typically for the transaction


What is first-level cache?
That same context (per persistence context, not app-wide)



Student a = em.find(Student.class, 1L);
Student b = em.find(Student.class, 1L);
// a == b  (same managed instance) inside same context
Second find often hits L1 cache → no second SELECT for same id.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 3 — Entity lifecycle states
          persist()
 transient ───────► managed ◄──── merge() (returns managed copy)
                       │  ▲
              remove() │  │ refresh / find again in new context...
                       ▼  │
                    removed    detached
                                 ▲
                                 │ clear() / transaction end / em.close()



State
Meaning




Transient
New Java object, not known to Hibernate yet


Managed
Tracked by persistence context; changes can auto-flush


Detached
Was managed; context no longer tracks it


Removed
Scheduled for DELETE on flush



Important: managed ≠ “SQL already ran.” Inserts/updates often wait until flush.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 4 — Dirty checking & flush
@Transactional
public void rename(Long id, String name) {
    Student s = em.find(Student.class, id); // managed
    s.setName(name);                        // dirty
} // end → flush → UPDATE → commit
Dirty checking: compare current field values to loaded snapshot
Flush:          push pending SQL to the database
Commit:         finish the DB transaction



Myth
Reality




Setter runs UPDATE immediately
Usually waits until flush


flush() == commit()
Flush writes SQL; commit ends transaction


detach() deletes the row
No — only stops tracking



Manual flush (rare in normal apps):
em.flush();  // SQL now, transaction still open
Batch tip: after many inserts, flush() + clear() keeps memory small.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 5 — Why @Transactional on the service
Spring starts a transaction, binds an EntityManager/Session to that work, then commits or rolls back.
Controller
   → Service proxy (@Transactional)
        begin TX + persistence context
        → repository / EntityManager calls
        flush + commit (or rollback)
Self-invocation note (same as AOP): calling this.method() inside the same class may skip the proxy → no new transaction boundary. Prefer calling through another Spring bean.

Which ops need a transaction?



Operation
Usually needs TX?




find (simple)
Often works read-only / auto


persist / merge / remove / flush
Yes



Put write methods in @Transactional service methods.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 6 — First-level cache limits
L1 helps same id lookups in one persistence context.
It does not:

Share across HTTP requests / different transactions by default

Automatically make every JPQL query use the cache the same way as find

Replace a second-level cache (separate topic)

Request A TX          Request B TX
 context A            context B
 (own L1)             (own L1)

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 7 — Handy EntityManager methods



Method
Plain use




persist
New entity → managed (insert later)


find
Load by PK (uses L1)


remove
Managed entity → delete later


merge
Copy detached state into a managed instance


flush
Sync SQL now


clear
Detach all (empty L1)


detach
Detach one


refresh
Reload from DB (overwrite memory)


contains
Is this instance managed here?

Topic 1 — execution pointcut (most common)
Shape:
execution( modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws? )

// any method in a package
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.*(..))

// any public method named save
execution(public * save(..))

// ProductService only
execution(* com.example.demo.service.ProductService.*(..))

// one arg
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.*(*))

// starts with get
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.get*(..))



Piece
Meaning




* return
any return type


.. in params
any number of args (including 0)


* in params
exactly one arg of any type


* in name/package
wildcard segment

section: Topic 4 — JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB
text:
Topic 4 — JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB
Bean implements an interface?
  │
  ├─ YES (classic Spring default story)
  │     JDK dynamic proxy
  │     - implements the same interface(s)
  │     - cast to interface type works
  │     - cast to concrete class may fail
  │
  └─ NO  (class only)  OR Boot often prefers CGLIB anyway
        CGLIB proxy
        - subclass of the concrete class
        - works without an interface

Practical rules

Prefer injecting the interface type (OrderService) not the impl class when you have one.

Final classes / methods are hard or impossible for CGLIB to override — advice may not apply.

Private methods are not advised by Spring AOP (only public calls through the proxy on Spring beans).

Self-invocation: this.helper() inside the same class bypasses the proxy → no advice on helper().

Wrong (self-call)                 Right
─────────────────                 ─────
@Service                          @Service
class S {                         class S {
  void a(){ this.b(); }             void a(){ other.b(); } // or inject self carefully
  void b(){ ... }  // no advice     ...
}                                 }

Response

text:
Why Filters? (cross-cutting for HTTP)
Cross-cutting = the same concern on many endpoints:

log method + URL + status

measure time taken

require an Authorization header

reject requests early

If you copy that into 20 controllers, you will miss endpoints. Filters sit outside controllers once.

  ▼

  │
  ▼

text:

Environment
Typical needs

H2 or local Postgres, verbose logs, maybe fake mail

real DB, less noisy logs, real secrets from env



Hard-coding localhost in Java breaks the day you deploy. Profiles keep environment details in config files.

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Topic 1 — YAML vs properties (same idea)
Both are Spring config. YAML is nested and often easier to read:
properties
server.port=8080
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:demo
YAML
server:
  port: 8080
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:demo
Indentation matters in YAML. Wrong spaces = startup fail.
You can keep .properties if you prefer. Profiles work with both:

application-dev.properties / application-dev.yml

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Topic 2 — Profile-specific files
src/main/resources/
  application.yml           # always loaded
  application-dev.yml       # when profile "dev" is active
  application-prod.yml      # when profile "prod" is active
Example application.yml:
spring:
  application:
    name: demo-api

server:
  port: 8080
Example application-dev.yml:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:devdb
  jpa:
    show-sql: true

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example: DEBUG
Example application-prod.yml:
server:
  port: 80

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db.example.com:5432/app
  jpa:
    show-sql: false

logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
Merge rule (simple mental model): base file loads first; active profile file(s) override matching keys.

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
section: Topic 3 — How to activate a profile
text:
Topic 3 — How to activate a profile

A) Inside config (good for local default)
spring:
  profiles:
    active: dev


B) IDE run configuration
IntelliJ / Eclipse: VM option or program arg:
-Dspring.profiles.active=dev
or
--spring.profiles.active=dev


C) Command line when running the jar
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod


D) Environment variable
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
Practical tip: do not bake prod as the only default in the repo. Prefer dev locally; set prod on the server.

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:

Controllers should not be full of try/catch.

Service throws ResourceNotFoundException

@RestControllerAdvice

JSON { message, status, ... } + 404

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling

Without it:







What clients see
Why it is bad




Default Whitelabel / stack-ish error
Ugly, inconsistent, sometimes leaks internals


Different controllers invent different error JSON
Front-end cannot rely on one shape


try/catch copy-paste
Business code gets noisy



With a global handler: one error contract for the whole API.

Risk
What goes wrong




Extra fields

Response may show password hashes, internal flags, relations


Coupling
Changing DB columns instantly changes your public API

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring MVC is still servlet-based.
One front controller — DispatcherServlet — receives every request, finds the right controller method, and builds the response (JSON or a JSP page).
Client → Tomcat → DispatcherServlet → Controller method → Response
Boot makes this easy. This lecture shows what Boot was hiding.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
section: Topic 1 — Spring MVC vs Spring Boot
text:
Topic 1 — Spring MVC vs Spring Boot







Piece
Role




Spring MVC (spring-webmvc)
Web framework: mapping, controllers, views, JSON


Spring Boot
Auto-configures MVC + embedded Tomcat + Jackson for you



Boot does not replace MVC. Your @GetMapping methods are MVC features.
Without Boot you would manually:

start Tomcat

create Spring web context

register DispatcherServlet

enable WebMvc / component scan

add Jackson

With Boot + spring-boot-starter-web, most of that appears automatically.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 2 — Why DispatcherServlet?
Pure servlet style: one servlet per URL family.
/student/create → CreateStudentServlet
/student/get    → GetStudentServlet
/student/update → UpdateStudentServlet
Each servlet repeats parsing, routing ideas, response writing…
Spring MVC idea:

One central servlet receives everything, then dispatches to the correct handler method.

That central servlet is DispatcherServlet. It is still a normal servlet Tomcat can call.
Traditional:  URL → YourServlet
Spring MVC:   URL → DispatcherServlet → @Controller method

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 3 — High-level request flow
Client HTTP request
        │
        ▼
Tomcat receives it
        │
        ▼
Tomcat calls DispatcherServlet
        │
        ▼
HandlerMapping: "which controller method?"
        │
        ▼
HandlerAdapter: "invoke that method"
        │
        ▼
Args resolved (@PathVariable, @RequestBody, …)
        │
        ▼
Controller → Service → Repository (your layers)
        │
        ▼
Return value handled
  ├─ REST: object → JSON (message converter)
  └─ MVC page: view name → ViewResolver → JSP
        │
        ▼
Client gets response
DispatcherServlet coordinates. Other components do specialized jobs.



Component
Job




DispatcherServlet
Front controller / coordinator


HandlerMapping
Map request → handler method


HandlerAdapter
Actually call the method


Argument resolvers
Fill method parameters


HttpMessageConverter
JSON ↔︎ Java (often Jackson)


ViewResolver
Logical view name → real page (JSP)

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 4 — HandlerMapping
DispatcherServlet does not hardcode “GET /students/1 means getStudent.”
At startup:

Component scan finds @RestController / @Controller

HandlerMapping reads @GetMapping, @PostMapping, …

Builds an internal table

GET    /students/{id}  → StudentController.getStudent
POST   /students       → StudentController.createStudent
PUT    /students/{id}  → StudentController.updateStudent
DELETE /students/{id}  → StudentController.deleteStudent
At runtime it looks up that table.
Same path + different HTTP method can mean different handlers (GET list vs POST create).

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 5 — HandlerAdapter
HandlerMapping finds the method.
HandlerAdapter runs it (prepare args, invoke, handle return).
DispatcherServlet
   asks Mapping  → "getStudent"
   asks Adapter  → "please call getStudent properly"

Path variable
GET /students/10 + @GetMapping("/{id}") + @PathVariable Integer id → id = 10


Query param
GET /students?name=Rohit + @RequestParam String name → name = Rohit


Request body
POST JSON + @RequestBody Student student → Jackson fills the object.
JSON bytes → HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) → Student
Student return value → converter → JSON response
No-arg constructor on the model helps Jackson construct objects.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:

Playlist index: 14

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Big idea in one line
Browsers speak HTTP, not Java.
Tomcat (a servlet container) receives HTTP and calls your Java servlet. Spring Boot embeds Tomcat so main() starts the server for you.
Browser ──HTTP text──► Tomcat ──calls──► Your Servlet (doGet/doPost/…)

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
section: Why this lecture after Boot CRUD?
text:
Why this lecture after Boot CRUD?
You already wrote @RestController methods. Under the hood, something still:

Listens on a port

Parses HTTP

Calls Java code

Writes an HTTP response

That “something” is the servlet world. Spring MVC sits on top of it (next lecture).

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 1 — Browser only sends HTTP
Opening http://localhost:8080/hello does not call HelloServlet.java directly.
The browser sends text roughly like:
GET /hello HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Java classes do not magically receive that. A server process must be listening on the port.

Could you use raw sockets?
Yes — ServerSocket on 8080. Then you manually parse URLs, headers, bodies, status codes, threads… forever.
Servlets exist so developers write business logic, not HTTP plumbing.
Without servlet container:
  Browser → raw socket code → you parse HTTP → you route → you write response

With servlet container:
  Browser → Tomcat → HttpServletRequest/Response → your Servlet class

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 2 — Static vs dynamic



Kind
Behavior




Static
Server returns an existing file (HTML/CSS/image)


Dynamic
Response depends on logic / DB / input (/user?id=101)



Dynamic needs Java (or another language). The missing link: how does HTTP enter Java? → Servlet.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 4 — Tomcat = Servlet Container
Tomcat is a Java server. More precisely: a Servlet Container.
“Container” means it creates, manages, and controls objects — like Spring’s IoC container manages beans.
Tomcat manages:

servlet creation

init / service / destroy

request & response objects

threads

URL mapping

sending the response


Inversion of control (again)



Style
Who is in charge




Normal Java
You new the object and call methods


Servlet world
Tomcat creates and calls


Spring world
Spring container creates and injects



Same IoC idea. Different container.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 5 — Request path through Tomcat
GET /myapp/hello
        │
        ▼
Tomcat: which app? → myapp
        which URL? → /hello
        which servlet? → HelloServlet
        which method? → doGet
        │
        ▼
helloServlet.doGet(request, response)
HttpServletRequest gives method, path, params, headers, body access.
HttpServletResponse lets you write status, headers, body.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 6 — Servlet lifecycle
create object → init() → service() → doGet/doPost/… → destroy()



Method
When
Typical use




init()
Once after creation
One-time setup


service()
Every request
HttpServlet routes to doXxx


doGet / doPost / …
Matching HTTP verb
Your logic


destroy()
Once before removal
Close resources



Default: servlet often loads on first request (then reused).
One servlet object usually serves many requests — be careful with mutable instance fields under concurrency.
First  GET /lifecycle → constructor, init, service, doGet
Second GET /lifecycle → service, doGet   (no second init)
Stop Tomcat           → destroy

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 7 — External Tomcat + WAR
Traditional flow:
Install Tomcat
  → build myapp.war
  → copy WAR into tomcat/webapps/
  → start Tomcat
  → app runs
Mental model: application goes inside Tomcat.

What is a WAR?
WAR = Web Application Archive. Packaged web app (classes, web.xml, static files, libs).
External Tomcat knows how to explode/run WARs under webapps/.
One Tomcat can host many apps:
/app1/hello  → servlet in app1
/app2/login  → servlet in app2


Start / stop (idea)



OS
Start
Stop




Windows
bin\startup.bat

Big idea in one line
Do not hardcode changeable values in Java.
Put them in config. Inject them into beans. Run startup code with a runner — not by hand from main.

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Why configuration files?
Tomorrow you may switch Razorpay → Stripe, or change retry count per environment.
If those values live inside a class:

Edit Java

Recompile

Rebuild

Redeploy

Painful for settings that change often.
Better place for them:

payment provider name

retry / timeout

feature flags

database URL / username

server port

Keep business logic in Java. Keep settings outside.

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Topic 1 — application.properties
Spring Boot loads this file by convention from:
src/main/resources/application.properties
Example:
payment.provider=Razorpay
payment.retry-count=3
payment.enabled=true
payment.timeout=5000
YAML works too (application.yml). Same idea, different writing style:
payment:
  provider: Razorpay
  retry-count: 3
  enabled: true
  timeout: 5000

Is this “external”?
The file inside src/main/resources is packaged into the JAR. Changing only that source file still needs a rebuild.
But Boot also reads overrides from outside the JAR:

environment variables

command-line args

system properties

external config files

Plain words: keep settings out of business methods so environments can differ without rewriting logic.
Dev:  payment.provider=TestProvider
Prod: payment.provider=Razorpay
Same PaymentService code in both places.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring Boot is still Spring.
It does not replace the IoC container. It starts the container for you and turns on smart defaults based on what JARs are on your classpath.
Spring Core (what you already learned)
  create context → scan components → make beans → inject deps

Spring Boot
  same steps
  + less startup code
  + "starters" (ready dependency packs)
  + auto-configuration (Boot adds useful beans when it makes sense)

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Why Boot after Core?
In Core you kept writing the same startup again and again:

Make ApplicationContext
Point it at a config class / XML
Put @ComponentScan (or list beans in XML)
Call getBean(...) yourself

That is fine for learning. In real apps it gets boring and easy to get wrong.
Boot’s job: keep the useful Spring Core behavior, remove the repeated setup.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: Picture: Core startup vs Boot startup
text:
Picture: Core startup vs Boot startup
SPRING CORE                              SPRING BOOT
────────────                             ───────────
main                                     main
  │                                        │
  ├─ new AnnotationConfig...               ├─ SpringApplication.run(App.class, args)
  │    (AppConfig.class)                   │
  ├─ @Configuration                        ├─ @SpringBootApplication on App
  ├─ @ComponentScan                        │     (includes scan + config + auto-config)
  ├─ beans created                         ├─ beans created (yours + Boot’s)
  └─ you call getBean / business code      └─ app keeps running (web server if web starter)
Same engine. Shorter ignition key.

Topic 2 — spring-boot-starter-parent (simple meaning)
Problem: many libraries must use matching versions.
If Web is version A and JDBC is version B, things break. Checking that by hand is painful.
Fix: Boot gives you a parent POM.
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version><!-- Boot version --></version>
</parent>

What the parent does for you







Without parent
With parent




You pick versions for every Spring-related dependency
Parent already knows a tested set of versions


Easy to mix incompatible JARs
Add starters without writing <version> most of the time



Plain words: the parent is a “version menu” Boot maintains so you do not fight dependency hell.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Topic 3 — spring-boot-starter (simple meaning)
A starter is a ready-made dependency pack.







Starter
Rough meaning




spring-boot-starter
Core Boot support (logging, auto-config engine, …)


spring-boot-starter-web
Web apps + embedded Tomcat + Spring MVC


spring-boot-starter-test
Testing tools



When you only add spring-boot-starter (no web), Tomcat does not start.
That is normal. Boot only pulls Tomcat when a web starter puts those classes on the classpath.
Remember: starters change what is available. Auto-config decides what Boot creates from that.

section: Topic 6 — Auto-configuration (the part that feels like magic)
text:
Topic 6 — Auto-configuration (the part that feels like magic)

Plain explanation

You add a starter → JARs appear on the classpath

Boot has a list of “if you have X, I can set up Y” rules

For each rule, Boot asks: should I turn this on?

If yes, Boot adds beans into the same IoC container as your beans

Classpath has Jackson?  ──yes──► maybe create JSON-related beans
Classpath has Tomcat + web? ──yes──► start embedded server setup
You already defined MyService? ──yes──► skip Boot’s default MyService


Two conditions you should know by name







Annotation
Plain meaning




@ConditionalOnClass
“Only if this class exists on the classpath”


@ConditionalOnMissingBean
“Only if you did not already define this bean”



Why @ConditionalOnMissingBean matters:
Boot gives defaults. You can override them by declaring your own @Bean / @Component of the same type. Boot then steps aside.
You define DataSource bean  → Boot’s default DataSource auto-config backs off
You define nothing          → Boot may create a default (when DB starter is present)


Your beans vs Boot’s beans








Kind
Who wrote the class
How it got into the container




App beans
You
@Component / your @Bean


Auto-config beans
Spring Boot / libraries
Enabled by @EnableAutoConfiguration + conditions



Same container. Different authors.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: Topic 7 — Why no Tomcat without Web?
text:
Topic 7 — Why no Tomcat without Web?
Common surprise:

“I run Boot, but there is no Tomcat on 8080.”

Because:

Auto-config looks at the classpath

Without spring-boot-starter-web, Tomcat / web MVC pieces are not there (or not selected)

So Boot does not start a web server

Add Web starter → Tomcat-related auto-config can turn on → you see a port again (like lecture 02).
Takeaway: Boot is not “always a web framework.” It becomes a web app when you pull web dependencies.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core

text:
How to reason when something fails
Ask in this order:

Is the class under the main package (or a sub-package)? → component scan

Is the starter on the classpath? → check pom.xml

Did I already define my own bean that blocks Boot’s default? → @ConditionalOnMissingBean

Am I expecting a web server without the web starter? → add Web or stop expecting port 8080

This is how you debug Boot without calling it “magic.”

<bean id="orderService"

Mode

Why this lecture matters (not syntax tourism)
If you only memorize annotations, you will still get lost when:

                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. Build ALL bean definitions FIRST                         │
│    Blueprint per type: name, class, scope, lazy flag,       │
│    dependency list — NO business objects yet for lazy/proto │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. Instantiate non-lazy singletons (dependency order)       │
│    constructor runs here                                    │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. Populate remaining DI (setter / field if any)            │
│    (constructor DI already happened in step 4)              │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 6. Aware callbacks (optional)                               │
│    BeanNameAware · ApplicationContextAware · …              │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 7. Initialization callbacks                                 │
│    @PostConstruct → InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()   │
│    → @Bean(initMethod=…)                                    │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 8. Bean ready — your app calls business methods             │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 9. Destruction callbacks (on context.close / shutdown)      │
│    @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy()                   │
│    → @Bean(destroyMethod=…)                                 │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 10. Bean destroyed / removed from active use                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Variants (same map, different cut-points):
@Lazy singleton
  steps 1–3 always
  steps 4–8 deferred until first getBean / first injection use
  steps 9–10 still apply when context closes (if bean was created)

prototype
  steps 1–3 always
  steps 4–7 when requested
  then Spring HANDS OBJECT TO CLIENT and stops managing it
  ⇒ steps 9–10 DO NOT run for that instance

Topic 1 — Container start & configuration (complete)

What “passing AppConfig.class” actually means
You do not pass an AppConfig instance into the container. You pass class metadata. Spring uses Java reflection to discover:

annotations on the class (@Configuration, @ComponentScan)
@Bean methods
which packages to scan

var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);


Minimal config you already know

@ComponentScan // same package as AppConfig if no basePackages given

}


Reasoning checkpoint







Question
Answer you should be able to give




Why reflection?
Container must discover annotations without you calling every setter by hand


When does scanning happen?
During context refresh / construction — before you call business methods


Is AppConfig itself a bean?
Yes — @Configuration is a @Component; Spring needs an instance to invoke @Bean methods



Do not leave this half-baked: until the context exists and config is read, no @PostConstruct on your services can run.

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 2 — Bean definition phase (complete)

What a bean definition is
A bean definition is the container’s blueprint for a bean — metadata before (or independent of) creating the instance:



Metadata
Examples




Bean name
default: camelCase class name (orderService)


Type
OrderService.class


Scope
singleton / prototype / …


Lazy flag
default false for singleton


Dependencies
constructor args, @Autowired points





Critical ordering rule
Spring builds definitions for all managed types first, then decides which objects to instantiate now.
Why?

Prototype → must not create at startup
@Lazy singleton → must not create at startup
Dependency graph → must know “Order needs Payment” before creating Order

Scan components
      │
      ▼
Create definitions for OrderService AND PaymentService
      │
      ▼
Only THEN instantiate the eager singletons (in dependency order)


Instantiation order is dependency-aware
Not random. If OrderService’s constructor needs PaymentService, Spring creates Payment first, then Order — even if scan discovered Order first.

Topic 8 — @Lazy singleton (complete variant)
Eager singleton:  definition → create now → … → ready at startup
Lazy singleton:   definition → WAIT → create on first use → … → ready
@Component
@Lazy
public class CartService { /* same as above */ }
Experiment

Mark CartService @Lazy.
Start context but do not getBean(CartService.class).
Observe: no constructor / @PostConstruct logs.
Then getBean → full remaining lifecycle runs.
context.close() → @PreDestroy runs if the bean was created.

When it is justified

Expensive bean rarely touched
Breaking a circular dependency with a lazy proxy (workaround — redesign still better)

When it is dangerous

Hides misconfiguration until first request (fails late)
“Make everything lazy for performance” is not a strategy

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 9 — Prototype scope (complete variant)
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.ConfigurableBeanFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;

@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class CartService { /* ... */ }

Lifecycle difference — finish this idea fully
Prototype request:
  create → inject → Aware → @PostConstruct → HAND OVER TO YOU
                                              │
                                              ▼
                         Spring forgets this instance
                         (no @PreDestroy from container)
Why? If Spring kept every prototype forever to call @PreDestroy later, it would retain references and risk memory leaks. So Spring initializes prototypes, then releases ownership.



Callback
Singleton
Prototype




Constructor
yes

@PostConstruct
yes
yes (each instance)


@PreDestroy
yes (on context close)
no (you clean up)



Robust-app rule: if a prototype holds a file/socket/pool, you must close it in your code (try-with-resources, explicit close(), custom tracking). Do not expect @PreDestroy.
Prove it in the lab: add @PreDestroy logging, use prototype scope, getBean twice, context.close() — destroy log should not appear for those instances.

Scope? singleton or prototype (or web scope)?

What resource must be released? → @PreDestroy only if Spring still manages this instance

Stateless services → singleton; no request-specific mutable fields
Constructors stay light
Init that needs deps → @PostConstruct
Every acquired resource has a matching release path

title: Lecture 6 — Circular dependency, bean scope, lazy & eager
text:
Concepts

Circular dependency
OrderService  ──needs──►  PaymentService
     ▲                         │
     └──────── needs ──────────┘
Spring creates beans in dependency order. With constructor injection on both sides, neither bean can finish constructing → typically BeanCurrentlyInCreationException (or a clear circular-reference error at context startup).








Approach
What happens
Verdict




Redesign (extract third type / events / break the cycle)
No cycle
Preferred


@Lazy on one constructor parameter
Injects a lazy proxy; real bean created later
Workaround


Setter / field injection
Partial object published, then wired
Workaround; hides design smell



Constructor injection is not “wrong” here — it surfaces the cycle early. That is a feature.


Side note from the lecture: @Configuration is a component
@Configuration is meta-annotated with @Component. The config class itself becomes a bean so Spring can invoke your @Bean methods. Component scanning + @Bean factories both live in the same container world you started in lecture 5.


Bean scope
Scope = how many instances Spring creates for a bean definition, and when.








Scope
Instances
Typical use




singleton (default)
One per bean definition
Stateless services


prototype
New instance every time the bean is requested
Stateful / per-use objects


request / session / application
Web-aware (later)
HTTP request/session lifetime









ImportantInterview-depth point



Singleton does not mean “only one object in the whole JVM / container.”
It means one instance per bean definition.
Two @Bean methods that both return OrderService → two singleton definitions → two instances, each reused when you ask for that definition.




Eager vs lazy initialization









Eager
Lazy




When created
When the container starts (for singletons by default)
On first request / first use


Default
Singleton → eager
Prototype → effectively lazy (created when asked)


Fail-fast
Config errors show at startup
Errors may hide until first use


Annotation
(default)
@Lazy on a bean or on an injection point



Tradeoff: eager = slower startup, faster discovery of broken wiring; lazy = faster startup, later failures.

title: Lecture 5 — Spring IoC container
text:
Concepts

Bean
A bean is an object created and managed by the Spring IoC container.
Not every Java object is a bean — only the ones the container knows about.


What the container does (replaces main wiring)
You declare types + relationships
            │
            v
   Spring IoC container
     • instantiate beans
     • inject dependencies
     • manage lifecycle
            │
            v
   Your code calls business methods


Two ways to tell Spring about beans








Approach
How you mark types
Typical use




Component scanning
@Component / @Service / @Repository / @Controller
Your own app classes


@Bean methods
Methods inside @Configuration
Third-party types, explicit factory setup



@Service, @Repository, @Controller are specializations of @Component (same scanning idea; clearer intent).


@Autowired
Asks Spring: “find a bean that matches this dependency and inject it.”

Match is usually by type
On a single constructor, Spring Boot / modern Spring can inject without writing @Autowired
If multiple constructors exist, mark the one Spring should use
If multiple beans of the same type exist, resolve with @Primary / @Qualifier (see exercises)



Component scan
Spring looks in configured packages for stereotype annotations.
Boot: scanning starts from the package of the @SpringBootApplication class — keep your components in that package or subpackages.

Goal

By the end you will have felt:

Programming to an interface.

title: Lecture 4 — Dependency Injection & IoC
text:
Concepts

Dependency
If OrderService needs EmailService to finish placeOrder(), then EmailService is a dependency of OrderService.


Tight coupling (the problem)
OrderService ──creates──► EmailService
Problems:

Cannot switch to SMS/Popup without editing OrderService
Hard to unit-test without sending real emails
OrderService does two jobs: business logic and object creation (SRP smell)



Loose coupling via interface
OrderService ──depends on──► NotificationService (interface)
                                      ▲
                      EmailService / SmsService / …
Still incomplete if OrderService itself does new EmailService().


Dependency Injection (DI)
Someone outside creates the dependency and passes it in (constructor or setter).
OrderService only uses NotificationService; it does not create it.


Inversion of Control (IoC)
Control of creating and wiring objects moves from the class to an external assembler (main today, Spring container tomorrow).
Rough relationship used in the lecture:







Term
Role




IoC
The broader idea — control of wiring is inverted


DI
A practical technique to achieve IoC


Spring IoC container
Automates creation, wiring, lifecycle of beans





Injection styles (this lecture)







Style
Idea




Constructor injection
Pass dependency in constructor (preferred for required deps)


Setter injection
setX(...) after construction


Field injection
Annotate fields — meaningful with Spring; deferred

title: Lecture 3 — Master Apache Maven
text:
Concepts

Why Maven exists
Hand-managing JARs does not scale:

Wrong versions
Missing transitive libraries
“Works on my machine” classpath chaos

Maven is a build + dependency + project tool. It downloads libraries, compiles, tests, and packages your app using a standard layout.


Standard project layout
my-app/
  pom.xml
  src/
    main/
      java/          ← application code
      resources/     ← application.properties, etc.
    test/
      java/          ← tests
  target/            ← build output (generated; do not edit)


Coordinates (GAV)
Every artifact is identified by:



Field
Example
Meaning




groupId
com.example
Organization / namespace


artifactId
demo
Project name


version
0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
Release version



Together: com.example:demo:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.


POM (Project Object Model)
pom.xml is the project’s declaration: coordinates, packaging (jar/war/pom), dependencies, plugins, Java version, parent BOM (Spring Boot parent often manages versions for you).


Repositories







Repo
Role




Maven Central
Public default remote repository


Local ~/.m2/repository
Cache of downloaded artifacts on your machine



First build downloads; later builds reuse the local cache.


Super POM vs effective POM

Super POM: Maven’s built-in defaults.
Your POM: What you write.
Effective POM: Merged result (your POM + parents + Super POM).
Inspect with: mvn help:effective-pom



Build lifecycle (default)
Important phases (in order):
validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy



Phase
What it roughly does




compile
Compile main sources


test
Run unit tests


package
Build the JAR/WAR in target/


install
Put the artifact into your local .m2


clean
Delete target/ (separate clean lifecycle)



Running a phase runs all previous phases in that lifecycle too (package implies compile + test, unless you skip tests).

Concepts you need while coding

Localhost, IP, and port







Idea
Plain meaning




IP address
Unique address of a machine on a network


localhost / 127.0.0.1
“This same computer”


Port
Number that routes traffic to one process on that machine (Chrome, Spotify, your app…)


Default Spring Boot port
8080 (changeable)



On the public internet, browsers often hit 443 (HTTPS). A reverse proxy may forward that to your app’s internal port (e.g. 8080). Locally you call the app port directly.


Spring Initializr

Embedded Tomcat
Adding Spring Web pulls in an embedded Apache Tomcat. When you run the main class, Tomcat listens on a port. You do not install Tomcat separately for this hello-world.

Annotation
Role in this lecture

On the generated main class — Boot entry point

Marks a class as an HTTP API “gateway”

Open https://start.spring.io
Choose roughly:








Field
Suggested choice




Project

A stable release (avoid SNAPSHOT / RC while learning)

Step 2 — run the skeleton once
Open the generated *Application.java (has public static void main).
Optionally add one line inside main before understanding Boot:
System.out.println("Hello World");
Run the main class. In the console logs you should see something like Tomcat started on port(s): 8080.

http://localhost:8080
You will likely see a Whitelabel Error Page — that is OK. It proves the server is up, but no endpoint is mapped yet.


Step 3 — create HelloController
In the same package as your main application class (e.g. com.example.demo), create:
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello World";
    }
}
What you are doing

@GetMapping("/hello") → “when someone GETs /hello, run this method”
Returning a String → Spring writes that string as the HTTP response body

Re-run the application (restart so changes load).
Visit:

http://localhost:8080/hello
Expected: page shows Hello World.


Step 5 — change the port
Open src/main/resources/application.properties and add:
server.port=9090
Restart. Tomcat should start on 9090. Now:
http://localhost:8080/hello   → fails (nothing listening)
http://localhost:9090/hello   → Hello World

Step 6 — second endpoint
Add another method (method name does not have to match the path):
@GetMapping("/bye")
public String greetBye() {
    return "Bye";
}
Restart and test both /hello and /bye.


Step 7 — optional HTML in the response
@GetMapping("/hello")
public String hello() {
    return "<h1>Hello World</h1>";
}
The browser will render the heading. (Real apps usually return JSON and let a frontend render HTML — that comes later.)

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
1. Setup from Lectures 2–3
We have the probability triplet \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and a random variable
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}
\]
(or later \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
Question of this lecture: what happens to the measure \(P\) when we pass to the range of \(X\)?

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 2. Which subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) do we use? Borel sets
text:
2. Which subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) do we use? Borel sets
Not every subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) is treated as an “event” in the range. We use a standard family: the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).
Intuition used in class: building blocks are half-lines of the form
\[
(-\infty,\ x]
\]
(and the \(\sigma\)-algebra they generate). In \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), the analogous building blocks are Cartesian products of such half-lines (rectangles unbounded toward \(-\infty\) in each coordinate).
Random variables are defined so that inverse images of these Borel sets land back in \(\mathcal{F}\) (measurability) — so probabilities remain well-defined.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
3. Pushforward measure = distribution of \(X\)
\(X\) maps outcomes in \(\Omega\) to numbers in \(\mathbb{R}\). Subsets of \(\Omega\) map (via inverse images) to subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\).
Because \(P\) lives on events in \(\Omega\), there is an induced measure on (Borel) subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\). That induced measure is called:



Name used in class
Same idea




Pushforward measure
\(P\) “pushed” through \(X\)


Distribution of \(X\)
law of \(X\)


Distribution function / CDF
common 1-D encoding of that law



Picture: one measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\) + a map \(X\) \(\Rightarrow\) a new measure space on the range side.

Course notation
Script / calligraphic \(P\) with a mark for \(X\) means the distribution of the random variable \(X\). In these notes we write \(P_{X}\).
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
4. Definition in one dimension (CDF view)
For \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) and a real number \(x\),
\[
P_{X}(x) \;=\; P\bigl( X^{-1}((-\infty,\ x]) \bigr) \;=\; P\bigl(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le x\}\bigr).
\]
In words:

Build the Borel set \((-\infty,\ x]\) in \(\mathbb{R}\).
Take its inverse image under \(X\) (a subset of \(\Omega\)).
Evaluate the original probability measure \(P\) on that event.

That value is the distribution function (CDF) at \(x\).
Endpoint convention: the interval is typically closed at \(x\) and open toward \(-\infty\), i.e. \((-\infty,\ x]\).

Probability is always assigned to a set (an event). Evaluating the distribution at \(x\) is still “probability of a set” — the set \(\{\omega : X(\omega)\le x\}\).
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 5. How is \(P\) “assigned” in the real world?
text:
5. How is \(P\) “assigned” in the real world?
Class answer: nature / the labeling process assigns the underlying measure. A radiologist’s intuition is hard to put into equations — we treat it as given by the problem.
Our engineering job (central theme of the course):

Given samples from the range of random variables, estimate the underlying distribution / measure.

That is the probabilistic formulation of ML that the next lectures will connect to function approximation.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 6. The working triplet from now on
text:
6. The working triplet from now on
Pushing forward gives a new triplet on the observation side, schematically
\[
\bigl(\mathbb{R},\ \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}),\ P_{X}\bigr).
\]
Once data are vectors from sensors, we mostly talk and compute in this pushforward world, while remembering that an underlying \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\) and map \(X\) sit behind it.
That is why random variables were invented: not decoration — the device that moves us from abstract \(\Omega\) to numbers with a well-defined distribution.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
7. Vector-valued random variables
In ML, usually
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}.
\]
(“Vector-valued RV” just means: the range consists of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\).)

Borel building blocks in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Cartesian products of half-lines, e.g. in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\):
\[
(-\infty,\ x_1] \times (-\infty,\ x_2].
\]
Geometrically: everything “southwest” of the point \((x_1,x_2)\) in the plane (with the usual closed/open conventions on edges).


Distribution at a vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Input to \(P_{X}\) is an element of the range of \(X\). For vector \(X\),
\[
P_{X}(x) \;=\; P\Bigl( X^{-1}\bigl( (-\infty,x_1]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,x_d] \bigr) \Bigr).
\]
Again: inverse image under \(X\), then apply \(P\).
Notation clash warning (from class): capital \(X\) for the RV vs small/bold \(x\) for a point in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) — same letter family, different objects.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
8. Distribution vs density (preview)

The distribution function / pushforward is a valid probability measure (on Borel sets).
A density (when it exists) is not itself a probability: evaluating a density at a single point does not give \(P(X=x)\) in continuous models.

Formal density discussion continues later; do not confuse “PDF value at a point” with “probability of an event.”
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 9. Multiple random variables (setup for next class)
text:
9. Multiple random variables (setup for next class)
There can be several random variables (hence possibly several experiments / sample spaces, or one joint experiment — your modeling choice).

X-ray + disease (two views)







View
Meaning




One experiment
“Get disease and get imaged” as a single process \(\to\) one \(\Omega\), maybe vector-valued \(X\)


Two experiments
Disease outcome vs imaging outcome as separate RVs that may be correlated



Both are allowed; random experiments are chosen by the modeler.


Vector RV vs many scalars
A Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) can be seen as:

one RV with range \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), or

\(d\) correlated scalar RVs (covariance / correlation matrix).

Same mathematics, two stories.


Discriminative vs generative (preview)
In this worldview they can look unified: the label is simply another coordinate of a vector-valued random variable; conditioning corresponds to restricting to appropriate events (set operations on the underlying spaces).
Next lectures: joint / conditional distributions more carefully, then ML as learning distributions (linked back to function approximation).
