title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
section: 3. Why we cannot stop at the triplet
text:
3. Why we cannot stop at the triplet
\(\Omega\) is often abstract and non-numeric (heads/tails; “someone got imaged and labeled”).
Engineers need numbers — we add, subtract, run algorithms, store arrays.
Slogan from class: think abstract, act concrete.

Thinking: probability space / experiment
Acting: concrete observations (vectors on a computer)

So we need a bridge from abstraction \(\to\) something we can compute with.

Sensors / observations (X-ray story)
Part of \(\Omega\): the whole story (nodule develops, person visits, imaging happens, …).
What we actually store: an X-ray image \(\to\) a vector on disk.
We work with vectors; we started from an abstract sample space. What connects them?
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
4. Random variable = the bridge
A random variable is a function
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}
\]
(or, more useful for ML, \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
It maps each abstract outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\) to a number (or vector) we can manipulate.

Why we need it







Without \(X\)
With \(X\)




Only abstract outcomes (H/T, “process happened”)
Concrete numbers / vectors


Hard to do algebra / ML
Can compute, fit models, store data



You cannot stop at \(\Omega\) if you want engineering work. The extra map \(X\) is not optional decoration — it is why RVs were defined.


Famous misnomer

A random variable is neither random nor a variable.
It is a deterministic function \(\Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)).

(Name is historical; treat it as a function.)


Range need not be all of \(\mathbb{R}\)

Can be integers, a finite set, etc.
In practice for images / features: range is \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Lecture generalizes: think \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
section: 5. What is a data point? (two layers of truth)
text:
5. What is a data point? (two layers of truth)

Deterministic language (Lecture 1)
An image is a point / vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\).


Probabilistic language (this lecture)
Still a point in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), but that \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is the range of a random variable \(X\) defined on an underlying sample space \(\Omega\) from a random experiment we do not fully observe.
Mental checklist whenever you see a datapoint \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\):
random experiment
      |
      v
sample space Omega
      |
      v
random variable X : Omega -> R^d
      |
      v
observed vector x  (element of the range of X)
Folder of images = many such range elements (realizations / observations of \(X\)).

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

6. Preview: what happens to \(P\)? (next ideas)
Defining \(X\) raises the natural question:

We had \(P\) on subsets of \(\Omega\). Under \(X\), what becomes of that measure on subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)?

Answer (named in class, developed next): pushforward measure, which becomes the distribution of \(X\).
Also mentioned: the image of the event \(\sigma\)-algebra under \(X\) relates to the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) (measure-theoretic detail — intuition: “nice” subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
This lecture stopped as that transition began; later parts fill in distribution / density.

text:
1. Bridge from Lecture 1
Last time: ML = function approximation.

Data: pairs from two sets
Assume unknown \(f\) maps domain \(\to\) range
Goal: estimate \(f\) (so we can predict on new inputs)

Prediction means: for a new \(x\) with unknown \(y\), use \(\hat{f}\) to guess \(y\).

Why that is not enough alone: for many problems you cannot derive \(f\) from physics (coin toss; reflectance \(\to\) “disease”). So we use a statistical / probabilistic approach: many observations, infer structure from data.

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
2. Why probability theory?
We must decide under uncertainty.
Irony stressed in class:

Inputs / world: uncertain
Final decisions (e.g. diagnosis): must be deterministic (A doctor cannot usefully stop at “60% diseased” without a decision rule.)

So we need a mathematical framework for uncertainty that still ends in decisions.

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
section: 3. Random experiment (where “random” starts — and almost ends)
text:
3. Random experiment (where “random” starts — and almost ends)
Probability begins with a random experiment:

An experiment whose outcomes we treat as uncertain / not fully predictable from our model of the world.

Important points from lecture:

“Randomness” itself is not rigorously defined — we assume we know what a random experiment is, then proceed with set theory / measure theory.
After fixing the experiment and its outcomes, almost nothing else is “random” — including random variables (coming soon): they are deterministic maps.
The designer chooses what counts as the experiment.

One toss of a coin
Five tosses of a coin Both are valid random experiments — different sample spaces.



Classic examples



Random experiment
Typical outcomes




Coin toss
\(\{H, T\}\)


Die roll
\(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\)





ML examples (see every datapoint this way)







Task
What is the “random experiment”? (intuition)




X-ray diagnosis
Person gets ill / seeks care \(\to\) imaging \(\to\) image on disk \(\to\) clinician label


Spam filter
Someone drafts/sends email \(\to\) someone labels spam / not


Brain measurement \(\to\) prediction
Person + protocol \(\to\) recorded signal



Punchline for ML: every training point is an outcome of an underlying random experiment. That is the probabilistic starting point.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
4. Sample space \(\Omega\)
Once the random experiment is fixed:
\[
\Omega = \{\text{all possible outcomes of the experiment}\}
\]
This set is the sample space.

Critical reminders

\(\Omega\) need not be numeric. Coin: \(\Omega = \{H,T\}\) — no numbers yet. X-ray pipeline: outcomes are abstract “whole process happened this way” objects — still not vectors until we define random variables (next lectures).
Sample space = enumerate outcomes in a set. Set theory begins here.


Don’t ask “what is randomness?” — collect outcomes into \(\Omega\), then work mathematically.

(Side joke from class: “random number generators” are deterministic algorithms \(\to\) pseudo-random.)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
5. Why measures? Comparing subsets
Having \(\Omega\) alone does not let us predict. We need to talk about how large / how likely subsets are.

Analogy: real numbers and length
On \(\mathbb{R}\), to say which of two intervals is “bigger,” we use length (Lebesgue measure on nice sets).

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): area
In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): volume
In \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \(d\)-dimensional volume

General idea: given a set, form subsets, assign a measure so we can compare / quantify them.
A measure is a mathematical function on (certain) subsets with formal properties (non-negativity, additivity for disjoint unions, etc.). This course gives the intuition; a full measure-theory course makes it airtight.


Back to \(\Omega\)
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a suitable collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events). Goal: assign a measure on members of \(\mathcal{F}\).
(In full rigor \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra — named in the lecture goals; formal axioms continue in the next parts.)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
6. Probability measure \(P\)
One special measure on events is the probability measure
\[
P : \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]
\]

Properties (as stated in class)
For events \(A,B \in \mathcal{F}\):

Non-negativity: \(P(A) \ge 0\)
Normalized on \(\Omega\): \(P(\Omega) = 1\)
Empty set: \(P(\emptyset) = 0\)
Additivity for disjoint events: if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), then

\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)
\]

Values lie in \([0,1]\) (unlike raw length, which can be arbitrarily large)

Analogy: think of \(P\) like “length,” but scaled so the whole sample space has measure 1.


Vocabulary



Term
Meaning




Outcome
An element of \(\Omega\)


Event
A subset of \(\Omega\) (element of \(\mathcal{F}\))


\(P(A)\)
Probability measure of event \(A\)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
section: 7. Meaning of \(P(A)\): optional until the end
text:
7. Meaning of \(P(A)\): optional until the end
Mathematically, \(P\) is just a measure with those axioms.
Common interpretation: \(P(A)\) = “likelihood” that event \(A\) occurs (e.g. \(P(A)=0.7\) \(\to\) “70% chance” in ordinary speech).
Lecture philosophy:

You can run almost all of the math of ML treating \(P\) as a pure abstraction.
Assign human meaning (diagnosis language, business risk, etc.) at the end, when a decision must be communicated.
Same measure, different stories in different applications — like “area under a curve” meaning different physical things in different sciences.

Abstraction payoff for ML: once data = values of random variables with an underlying \(P\), the same algorithms apply to images, text, time series, brain signals — all are vectors in the range of those maps. That is why a “generalist” ML view is possible.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
1. What this course is for
This is the first of a two-course series:







Course
Role




This one
Mathematical / probabilistic foundations of ML


Next semester
State-of-the-art algorithms (esp. generative models)



Goal: move from “internet data scientist” (drive the car) to someone who can build and reason about algorithms (design the engine).
Analogy used in class:

You don’t need to know how an internal combustion engine works to drive a car.
You do need that knowledge if you want to build a better one.

By the end, reading an ML paper should feel closer to reading a novel than decoding opaque jargon.
Teaching style: mostly chalk-and-board (no slides). Mathematics is treated as a language of precision — English is too ambiguous for engineering implementation.
Viewpoint: almost everything will be developed from a probabilistic standpoint (with deterministic parallels pointed out along the way).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
2. The central problem: function approximation
Most problems in science and engineering can be cast as function approximation.

Classical motivation
Kepler / Gauss-era question: observe planet positions at some times → predict positions at other times.

Independent variable: time → call this \(x\)
Dependent variable: position → call this \(y\)



Formal setup
Two sets:

Domain set \(\mathcal{X}\) (often called “input”; here we keep it abstract)
Range set \(\mathcal{Y}\) (often called “output”)

We are given a dataset of paired observations:
\[
\mathcal{D} = \bigl\{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\bigr\}
\]
where each \(x_i \in \mathcal{X}\) and \(y_i \in \mathcal{Y}\).
Assumption: there exists a function
\[
f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}
\]
such that the observations are (related to) evaluations of \(f\).
Problem: \(f\) is unknown.

Machine learning in one line (deterministic view):
Given \(\mathcal{D}\), find / estimate \(f\).

This is an ill-posed / “blind” problem: we only have samples, not a description of \(f\).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 3. How humans solve blind problems (the philosophy)
text:
3. How humans solve blind problems (the philosophy)
If you know nothing about \(f\), you cannot magically recover “truth.” The workable philosophy is:

Start with an initial guess on \(f\) (a model family)
Refine that guess using data \(\mathcal{D}\) (a learning algorithm)


Example: planetary motion
Kepler assumed orbits are ellipses. That does not finish the job — there are infinitely many ellipses. Data tells you which ellipse (among the family) fits.


Vocabulary that will stick for the whole course







Everyday phrase
ML meaning




Initial guess / family of candidates
Model / model family


Procedure that improves the guess with \(\mathcal{D}\)
Learning algorithm


Dataset \(\mathcal{D}\)
Data (“data is the new oil” — quality of \(\mathcal{D}\) limits quality of \(\hat{f}\))



Famous proverb cited in lecture:

All models are wrong, but some are useful.

We never have access to “true reality”; we only get estimates. The course will define what “useful” means rigorously later (error, risk, generalization, etc.).


Model families you will meet later
Different guesses on \(f\):

Linear models

Quadratic / polynomial families

Kernel machines

Decision trees

Neural networks

Different refinement algorithms (examples):

Least squares

Error backpropagation (for neural nets)

“Learning” = choosing a family + refining it with data. Both will be formalized later.


Overfitting (preview)
A bad “solution”: define \(\hat{f}(x_i) = y_i\) only at observed points and invent nonsense elsewhere.
That memorizes \(\mathcal{D}\) but fails the real goal: predict for unseen \(x\).
This idea will later be formalized as overfitting.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 4. Domains need not be scalars — think vectors
text:
4. Domains need not be scalars — think vectors
Nothing forces \(x\) or \(y\) to be single numbers. We often work with vector-valued inputs/outputs.

Running example: chest X-ray diagnosis

\(x_i\): an X-ray image

\(y_i \in \{0,1\}\): diseased / not diseased

In a computer, an image is a \(P \times Q\) matrix of pixel intensities (e.g. \(0\)–\(255\) for 8-bit).
Stack columns into one long vector of length \(PQ\). Then:
\[
x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{PQ}
\]
Abstractly, for the rest of the course:
\[
x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\]
(a point in \(d\)-dimensional Euclidean space).
The unknown \(f\) maps a high-dimensional image to a label \(\{0,1\}\).
In the real world, that \(f\) is roughly “what a radiologist does.”
ML tries to mimic such maps — this is the universal function approximation ambition: learn useful maps between complicated spaces.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
5. Why a probabilistic viewpoint?
Many ML methods can be told in a deterministic “fit a curve” language. That is not enough for the hard cases.

Measurable physics vs abstract human constructs
Easy (Newtonian) maps:

Force ↔︎ acceleration (linear, few parameters)

Enough to fly an aircraft with a small model

Hard maps:

Pixel reflectance → gender, disease, intent

Microphone pressure waveform → phoneme / meaning

A microphone measures pressure gradients. A camera measures reflected/absorbed radiation.
Why those numbers should equal an abstract label like “gender” or “phone /ah/” is not a simple physics formula with 5 parameters. Human semantics are complex; models may need millions of parameters.
Thought experiment (assignment-style): take MNIST digits and randomly shuffle labels. You can still train a model that fits those random labels. Semantics are subtle; memorization is possible; meaning is not automatic.


Historical lesson: speech recognition
For decades, speech scientists tried physics-first inversion:

Model vocal tract as waveguides / constrictions

Invert from waveform → articulatory configuration → phone

Hard and brittle.
In the late 1980s, statistical methods solved practical digit / speech recognition by:

Making many observations

Estimating patterns from data

Physics-first researchers sometimes called this “ignorance modeling.”
Engineers replied: but it works.
Modern deep learning sits in that lineage: systems that work at scale, even when full interpretability lags behind.


Takeaway
When \(f\) is too complex to derive from first-principles physics:

Make repeated observations and estimate \(f\) with statistical / probabilistic methods.

That is why this course is grounded in probability theory.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 6. From deterministic sets to random variables
text:
6. From deterministic sets to random variables
Deterministic view: \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}\) are sets; \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\); given \(\mathcal{D}\), estimate \(f\).
Probabilistic view: \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) are (supports of) random variables.
Function approximation becomes closely related to distribution / density estimation.
There will be one-to-one parallels between:







Deterministic language
Probabilistic language




Estimate unknown \(f\)
Estimate distributions / conditionals involving \(X,Y\)


Model family
Parametric / structured distributions


Fit with data
Inference / learning from samples



Generative models, in particular, are most natural in the probabilistic language. That language is broad enough to cover both discriminative and generative formulations (terms to be defined soon).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
7. Preparation for Lecture 2+
Refresh thoroughly before the next class:

Random experiment & sample space

Random variable (as a measurable function from sample space → \(\mathbb{R}\))

Probability measure

Distribution functions

Density functions (and that densities do not always exist)

Familiarity with measure-theoretic language (σ-algebras, etc.) will help — the course gets rigorous

Next lectures connect today’s function-approximation story to random variables and distribution estimation.

Observations D = {(x_i, y_i)}
        |
        v
Assume unknown map f : X -> Y exists
        |
        v
Choose a model family (initial guess)
        |
        v
Refine with data (learning algorithm)
        |
        v
Get useful estimate f̂  (not "truth")
When physics of \(f\) is unavailable → use statistics / probability and lots of data.

State the function approximation problem in one sentence using \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(f\).

What is the difference between a model family and a learning algorithm? Give one example of each.

In one sentence: how does the probabilistic view rephrase “estimate \(f\)”?

title: Lecture 1 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Course: Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning (Prof. Prathosh A.P.)
Based on: Lec 01 — Overview of Function Approximation



Create a tiny dataset (like observations in the lecture)
Make an initial guess for the unknown function (a model family)
Refine that guess using data
See overfitting (memorizing data)
See that a flexible model can even fit random labels
Turn a small “image” into a vector (X-ray idea from class)





Read each markdown cell (the text explanations).
Run the code cell right below it (Shift + Enter).
Do not skip cells — later cells need earlier ones.


You do not need to know ML already. If a line of code is new, the text above it explains what it does.




We need two libraries:



Library
Job




numpy
Work with numbers and arrays (lists of numbers)


matplotlib
Draw plots



If the next cell fails with ModuleNotFoundError, run this once in a cell:
%pip install numpy matplotlib
Then run the import cell again.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print("Imports OK. numpy version:", np.__version__)




In class we said:

We have pairs (x, y). We assume there is an unknown function f such that y ≈ f(x).
Goal: estimate f from data.

In this notebook we will pretend the true function is a sine wave:
\[
f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)
\]
In real ML we do not know f. Here we keep it secret from the “learner”, but we plot it as a dashed line so you can see the truth.

def true_f(x):
    """The unknown reality. In real problems we do NOT know this."""
    return np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)

# Try it on a few numbers
print("f(0.0) =", true_f(0.0))
print("f(0.25) =", true_f(0.25))  # should be about 1
print("f(0.5) =", true_f(0.5))    # should be about 0




Lecture notation:
\[
\mathcal{D} = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\}
\]
We will: 1. Pick random x values between 0 and 1 2. Compute y = true_f(x) 3. Add a little noise (real measurements are never perfect)
New words - seed: makes “random” numbers repeatable (same result every run) - noise: small random error added to y

def make_dataset(n=15, noise=0.15, seed=0):
    """Make n noisy observations from true_f."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)          # random number generator
    x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n))      # n random x in [0,1], sorted
    y = true_f(x) + rng.normal(0, noise, size=n)  # true value + noise
    return x, y

x_train, y_train = make_dataset()

print("Number of points:", len(x_train))
print("First 5 x values:", x_train[:5])
print("First 5 y values:", y_train[:5])




Red dots = what we observed (D)
Black dashed curve = true f (unknown in real life)

Notice: the dots are near the curve, but not exactly on it, because of noise.

x_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)  # many x values for a smooth curve

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", label="true f (unknown in real ML)")
plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, c="red", label="data D", zorder=3)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title("Observations vs the unknown function")
plt.legend()
plt.show()





From class:

Start with a guess for f (choose a model family)
Refine using data D

Our simple guess family: polynomials



Degree
Example shape




1
straight line: \(a + bx\)


2
parabola: \(a + bx + cx^2\)


3
cubic: \(a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3\)


high
can wiggle a lot



np.polyfit = refine the guess (find best coefficients for that degree)
np.polyval = use the fitted polynomial to predict y at new x

def fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, x_query, degree):
    """
    Guess family: polynomials of this degree.
    Refine: least squares fit to the data.
    """
    coeffs = np.polyfit(x_train, y_train, degree)  # learn coefficients from D
    y_hat = np.polyval(coeffs, x_query)            # predict on new x
    return y_hat

# Quick test: fit a line (degree 1) and predict at x=0.5
y_at_half = fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, 0.5, degree=1)
print("Degree-1 model prediction at x=0.5:", float(y_at_half))




We try three model families on the same data:



Degree
What usually happens




1
Too simple → underfitting (misses the curve)


3
Often a reasonable compromise


12
Too flexible → overfitting (chases noise, wild wiggles)



Overfitting matches what the lecture said: defining the function only to match observed points does not help on new x.

degrees = [1, 3, 12]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5), sharey=True)

for ax, deg in zip(axes, degrees):
    y_hat = fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, x_grid, degree=deg)

    ax.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", lw=1.5, label="true f")
    ax.plot(x_grid, y_hat, lw=2, label=f"degree {deg}")
    ax.scatter(x_train, y_train, c="red", zorder=3, label="data D")
    ax.set_title(f"Guess family: poly degree {deg}")
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

axes[0].set_ylabel("y")
fig.suptitle("Same data D — different initial guesses (model families)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Left plot: line cannot bend with the sine wave → bad guess family.
Middle: closer to truth → useful model (still “wrong”, but useful).
Right: passes near every red point, but oscillates → memorizing noise.

Lecture proverb: All models are wrong, but some are useful.




In class: take MNIST digits, shuffle the labels randomly, and you can still fit a powerful model.
Here we do a tiny version:

Meaningful labels: 1 if true_f(x) > 0, else 0
Random labels: coin-flip 0/1 with no meaning

We use a very flexible polynomial (degree 18).
Point: fitting the training points does not mean the labels make sense.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 20)
y_meaningful = (true_f(x) > 0).astype(float)          # structured 0/1 labels
y_random = rng.integers(0, 2, size=len(x)).astype(float)  # nonsense labels

print("Meaningful labels:", y_meaningful)
print("Random labels:    ", y_random)


y_hat_meaningful = fit_and_predict(x, y_meaningful, x_grid, degree=18)
y_hat_random = fit_and_predict(x, y_random, x_grid, degree=18)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), sharey=True)

axes[0].scatter(x, y_meaningful, c="C0", label="meaningful labels")
axes[0].plot(x_grid, y_hat_meaningful, c="C0")
axes[0].set_title("Fit meaningful labels")
axes[0].set_xlabel("x")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

axes[1].scatter(x, y_random, c="C1", label="random labels")
axes[1].plot(x_grid, y_hat_random, c="C1")
axes[1].set_title("Fit random labels (still possible!)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("x")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 1.2)

fig.suptitle("Flexible models can memorize nonsense")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This is why the course moves to a probabilistic view later:
we need ideas beyond “draw a curve through the points” (generalization, uncertainty, distributions).



In lecture: a \(P \times Q\) image → stack columns → one long vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{PQ}\).
We use a tiny fake “image” (4 rows × 5 columns) so you can see every number.

P, Q = 4, 5
img = np.arange(P * Q).reshape(P, Q)  # numbers 0..19 arranged as a grid

print("Image shape (rows, cols):", img.shape)
print("Image (matrix):")
print(img)


# order="F" means Fortran-order = stack COLUMN by column (as in lecture)
vec = img.reshape(-1, order="F")

print("As a vector in R^{}:".format(P * Q))
print(vec)
print("Vector length:", vec.shape[0])

plt.figure(figsize=(3, 3))
plt.imshow(img, cmap="viridis")
plt.title("Tiny fake image")
plt.colorbar()
plt.show()

A real X-ray is the same idea with a much bigger \(P\) and \(Q\)
(for example \(512 \times 512\) → a vector of length \(262\,144\)).
Then ML learns a function:
\[
f : \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \{0,1\}
\]
(image vector → diseased / not diseased).



Change numbers and re-run. There is no single “correct” answer — watch what happens.

# Exercise A: more noise → harder to see the true curve
x2, y2 = make_dataset(n=15, noise=0.4, seed=0)  # try noise=0.05 vs 0.4

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", label="true f")
plt.scatter(x2, y2, c="red", label="noisier data")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Exercise A: change the noise")
plt.show()


# Exercise B: change the degree yourself
my_degree = 5  # try 0, 2, 8, 14 ...

y_hat = fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, x_grid, degree=my_degree)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", label="true f")
plt.plot(x_grid, y_hat, label=f"degree {my_degree}")
plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, c="red", label="data D", zorder=3)
plt.legend()
plt.title("Exercise B: pick your own model family")
plt.show()







Lecture phrase
What we did




Dataset \(\mathcal{D}\)
red points (x_train, y_train)


Unknown \(f\)
true_f (sine)


Initial guess / model family
polynomial degree


Refine using data
np.polyfit


Overfitting
very high degree chasing noise


Random labels
flexible model fits nonsense


Image as vector
reshape matrix → long list of numbers


Why probability next?
fitting alone is not enough



Next lectures: probability theory — sample space, random variables, distributions.
When you finish, send the Lecture 2 link and we will make the next notes + notebook.

title: Lecture 3 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 03.


Sample space can be abstract (H / T).
A random variable is a function that turns those outcomes into numbers.
Run cells with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np

print('Ready')





Omega = sample space

Events = subsets

P = probability measure

Example: fair coin, Omega = {H, T}.

Omega = {"H", "T"}

def P(event):
    event = set(event)
    return sum(0.5 for o in event if o in Omega)

print("Omega =", Omega)
print("P({H}) =", P({"H"}))




We cannot do much arithmetic with the labels H and T.
Define a map X: Omega -> real numbers, for example:

X(H) = 1

X(T) = 0

That map is the random variable (a deterministic function!).

def X(omega):
    """Random variable: abstract outcome -> number."""
    return 1 if omega == "H" else 0

for outcome in sorted(Omega):
    print(f"X({outcome}) = {X(outcome)}")




When we “observe” many coin tosses, we store numbers (0/1), not the letters.
Those numbers are elements of the range of X.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# simulate abstract outcomes, then map through X
abstract = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=10)
data = np.array([X(o) for o in abstract])

print("Abstract outcomes:", abstract)
print("Observed data (range of X):", data)
print("Mean of data ≈ P(H) for fair coin:", data.mean())




For images, X maps Omega -> R^d (a long vector of pixels).
Tiny demo: pretend each outcome maps to a 2-D “feature vector”.

def X_vec(omega):
    # toy features: [is_heads, bias_term]
    return np.array([1.0, 1.0]) if omega == "H" else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

print("X_vec(H) =", X_vec("H"))
print("X_vec(T) =", X_vec("T"))
print("shape:", X_vec("H").shape)  # like a mini R^2 datapoint





# Exercise A: redefine X so X(H)=+1 and X(T)=-1 (common coding).
# Compute the average of 5000 simulated values. What do you expect for a fair coin?

def X_pm(omega):
    return 1 if omega == "H" else -1

sim = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=5000)
vals = np.array([X_pm(o) for o in sim])
print("sample mean:", vals.mean())  # expect near 0


# Exercise B: die Omega = {1,...,6}, X(omega)=omega (identity).
# This is already numeric — but still formally a random variable Omega -> R.

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

def X_die(omega):
    return float(omega)

print([X_die(o) for o in sorted(Omega_die)])

cannot stop at H/T labels


Random variable
function X: Omega -> R or R^d


Datapoint
value in the range of X
